You've seen the numbers. Each component works. The precedents are real. The math checks out. So the natural next question is the one your species reaches for whenever it is about to do nothing: "If this is so obvious, why hasn't someone smarter done it already?"

They have. Many times.

## People Have Tried This

Jeffrey Sachs has been arguing for massive health spending redirects since the 1990s. The WHO Commission on Macroeconomics and Health published a 200-page report in 2001 combining health economics with development economics to argue for exactly this kind of reallocation. Bjorn Lomborg's Copenhagen Consensus has been ranking global priorities by cross-domain ROI since 2004. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons won a Nobel Peace Prize in 2017. "Spend less on war, more on health" is not a new idea. Your species has been saying it out loud, with data, for decades.

So the question isn't "why hasn't anyone thought of this?" It's "why hasn't it worked?"

## Every Previous Attempt Had the Same Problem

Sachs proposed the spending. The WHO documented the returns. Lomborg ranked the priorities. ICAN built the coalition. Each one got further than the last. None of them stuck. And they all stalled for the same reason: they relied on governments choosing to act against the interests of their largest donors, indefinitely, out of conviction.

That is not how your species works. I have been watching you for a while and I can confirm: you do the right thing approximately when it is also the profitable thing, and not one moment sooner. You are not cruel. You are just on a schedule, and the schedule is money. Every successful precedent in [the proof chapter](../proof.qmd) confirms this. War bonds worked because grandma got 4% returns. The landmine treaty worked because weapons manufacturers didn't make landmines (their margins were in bigger weapons). The Global Fund worked because it was cheaper than letting AIDS destabilize trade partners. In each case, the moral argument was necessary but not sufficient. The financial mechanism made it stick.

Previous proposals said: "this is the right thing to do." This book says: "this is the right thing to do, and here is a [bond structure](../solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) that makes billionaires richer for doing it, a [decentralized FDA](../solution/dfda.qmd) [@dfda-spec-paper-2025; @dfda-impact-paper-2025] that makes trials cheaper, and a [governance mechanism](../solution/wishocracy.qmd) that makes corruption structurally unprofitable." The difference is not the diagnosis. The difference is the engine.

## The Combination Falls Between Every Institution's Brand

Your policy institutions could have assembled this. They have the economists, the data, and permission to think about more than one thing at once. But this proposal requires combining libertarian ideas (decentralize the FDA, cut government bureaucracy), progressive ideas (international cooperation, health as a right), and bond math ([incentive alignment](../solution/aligning-incentives.qmd)) simultaneously. That doesn't fit in any of your boxes. Disease, unfortunately, did not read your boxes.

Think tanks sell ideological consistency. This proposal doesn't fit in any box, because disease doesn't respect your political categories. It just kills you. The organizations that could do this analysis are funded by people who care very much about left versus right, so the analysis stays in its lane, and nobody combines the lanes. Not because they can't. Because half their donors would cancel their funding before the first footnote, and a think tank that solves the problem is a think tank that has to find a new problem.

## The Compound Math Is the Hard Part (Honestly)

Each individual mechanism is well-documented. Peace dividends, trial efficiency, disease burden reduction, research spillover. No serious economist disputes any of them in isolation. The uncertain part is the stacking: whether three or four mechanisms compound multiplicatively over 20 years, producing {{< var wishonia_trajectory_gdp_year_20 >}} (roughly {{< var wishonia_trajectory_gdp_vs_current_trajectory_multiplier_year_20 >}} the Earth baseline, or {{< var wishonia_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}} average income versus {{< var current_trajectory_avg_income_year_20 >}} on the current path).

That number makes economists stop reading. Some of that skepticism is pattern-matching against fraud. But some of it is legitimate. The independence assumptions are strong. The governance reform multiplier is the least certain component. The ratchet schedule is historically grounded but still speculative. The [GDP trajectories](../economics/gdp-trajectories.qmd) [@gdp-trajectories-paper-2025] chapter shows the work. But "transparent" is not the same as "certain."

Even the pessimistic math says trying beats not trying by an embarrassingly wide margin. You don't need to believe in 29x to believe that redirecting 1% of the murder budget to clinical trials is a good bet. The compound effect is the upside case. The [worst-case scenario](../proof.qmd#failsafe) (total mismanagement, every dollar wasted) still leaves you with fewer weapons and more data. You have to work hard to make this a bad deal.

## Why This Time Might Be Different

Previous attempts had the right diagnosis and no engine. This proposal has the engine: a [bond structure](../solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) that makes everyone's selfishness point in the same direction. Not because they all care about health. Because they all care about money, and the bond makes health the most profitable option.

Whether that engine actually works is an empirical question, not a rhetorical one. This chapter cannot answer it. Only the [treaty](../solution/1-percent-treaty.qmd) can answer it, if it gets signed. Which brings you back to the [two futures](../futures.qmd) and the only question that matters: whether knowing the math changes what you do next. One path requires action. The other requires nothing at all. Nothing is your species' best event. You have never lost at it.
